summary:
Project: Icarus – From Earth to Mars is an educational spaceflight simulator designed to show why launching a rocket and reaching another planet is one of the hardest engineering feats in human history. Developed for the NASA Space Apps "Space Mission Design Game" challenge, the game tasks players with executing critical Mars missions—such as investigating an anomalous impact near Jezero Crater, deploying surface rovers to search for ancient biosignatures, or retrieving geological sample caches.
To make the realities of spaceflight intuitive, Project: Icarus models real aerospace bottlenecks using NASA open data—including planetary fact sheets, historical engine metrics, and Sutton–Graves heating equations. Players experience firsthand why space access is so unforgiving: overcoming the "tyranny of the rocket equation" (balancing propellant mass against thrust across stages), surviving peak aerodynamic stress (Max-Q) during Earth ascent, enduring a 210-day deep-space cruise, and surviving the "seven minutes of terror" during Martian atmospheric entry and landing.
Through an iterative loop—Research, Build, Fly, and Debrief—players unlock 90 technologies, assemble 50 parts within strict mass budgets, and inspect telemetry logs after every crash. By turning failure into actionable engineering feedback, the game transforms complex physics into hands-on STEM education.
details:
1. The Project
Project Icarus is a space mission simulation game centered around rocket engineering and spacecraft design. To complete the mission—currently set on reaching Mars to investigate an unknown anomaly—players must engineer a launch vehicle capable of surviving the journey.
The gameplay revolves around a continuous "Design – Test – Fail – Learn" loop. With every launch attempt, players actively practice engineering and problem-solving skills while discovering how real space missions are planned, how rockets are structured for deep-space travel, and the fascinating aerospace principles behind them.


2. Why We Chose This Project
Space exploration and aerospace engineering are endlessly fascinating, yet they are often overlooked because of their steep technical barrier. While the meticulous planning and execution behind a real launch are breathtaking, most people—especially students—struggle to push through dense equations and dry textbook theory.
We chose this project to share our passion for the science behind spaceflight. A game is far more approachable than a textbook: it lets players experience complex concepts hands-on and see directly how the mechanics work in practice. Our goal is to spark curiosity in science, engineering, and aerospace—and hopefully inspire the next generation of future engineers.

3. How We Made It
We built Project Icarus in Godot 4 using C#, chosen for its lightweight footprint, fast prototyping workflow during a hackathon, and broad accessibility across everyday hardware. All custom 3D assets were modeled in Blender using a clean low-poly art direction—allowing us to iterate quickly, keep frame rates smooth, and give the game a welcoming, approachable look.
Because our goal is to help players learn, the core mechanics are grounded in real data and technical parameters from NASA and its partners, carefully calibrated so the simulation stays fun, intuitive to pick up, and rewarding to master. Beyond building the rocket's exterior structure, players also progress through a Research Tree modeled after real aerospace R&D—learning what scientific instruments go inside a spacecraft and what role each one plays in completing the mission.

4. A Final Note from Our Team
We hope Project Icarus shows that space missions and engineering aren't just about memorizing numbers and formulas—they are about thoughtful planning, creative testing, and resilient problem-solving. Above all, we hope this game gives players an accessible foundation in aerospace and inspires them to keep exploring. Thank you for checking out our project—we hope you enjoy playing it!
